uncited: It solves the problem of differentiating the analytic approximation used in [Analytic-Splatting](8084-analytic-splatting.md), which integrates the Gaussian density over the pixel area to reduce aliasing.
The covariance matrix is symmetric positive definite.
It is decomposed into eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ and corresponding unit eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$.
**Compute Eigenvector Gradients:** Calculate the gradient of the intensity with respect to each eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_k$ ($k \in \{1, 2\}$).
*   **Degenerate Eigenvalues:** If $\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2$, the eigenvectors are not unique, and the gradient $\frac{\partial \mathbf{v}_k}{\partial \hat{\Sigma}}$ becomes unstable.
*   **Boundary Derivatives:** The derivative of the CDF $S_{\sigma_2}$ is the Gaussian PDF.
*   **Time Complexity:** The gradient computation is dominated by the eigen-decomposition of the $2 \times 2$ covariance matrix, which is $O(1)$ per splat.
The evaluation of the Gaussian PDFs and CDF derivatives is also $O(1)$.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ auxiliary memory per splat for storing intermediate values ($\mathcal{I}_{\sigma 1}, \mathcal{I}_{\sigma 2}$) and gradients.
*   **Strengths:** Provides exact gradients for the analytic integration, enabling stable training of the covariance parameters without finite-difference approximations.
*   **Limitations:** Requires careful handling of degenerate eigenvalues ($\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2$) to avoid numerical instability in eigenvector gradients.
The computation is more complex than point-sampling gradients due to the boundary terms.
It was developed to address the aliasing artifacts in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting by providing a differentiable analytic approximation of the Gaussian integral over the pixel area.
